chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qassani, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Manqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: He was asked about the distribution of the treasury (bayt al-mal), so he said: 'The people of Islam are the children of Islam. I equalize among them in the stipend (ata'), and their virtues are between them and God; I group them together like the sons of one man, not preferring any one of them over another in inheritance due to his excellence or righteousness, if the other is weak or deficient.'

And he said: 'This is the action of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) at the beginning of his affair. And others among us, whom we precede, say: We prioritize them in the stipend based on what God has favored them with due to their precedents in Islam. If they were in Islam, they attained that, so we assign them according to the inheritance of those of kinship, some being closer to others, and having a larger share due to their closeness to the deceased. And they were inherited through their kinship, and that is what Umar used to do.'

key_terms.بَيْتُ الْمَالِ: The state treasury or public funds

ai.seo_question: How did the Imams and Umar differ in distributing the state treasury and inheritance among Muslims?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) articulates the foundational Sunni-Shia divergence regarding bayt al-mal distribution: while the Prophet Muhammad and early practice emphasized egalitarianism among all Muslims regardless of merit, Umar ibn al-Khattab introduced a meritocratic hierarchy favoring the Sahaba. This narration highlights the theological tension between the principle of equal brotherhood in Islam and the historical reality of prioritizing early converts, a distinction that remains central to Shia jurisprudence on public finance.
